newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq criticises Jordan over call for new policies.
newsitem.headline: Iraq criticises Jordan over call for new policies.

text.p: Iraq on Thursday branded Jordan's Information Minister Marwan Muasher "a false witness" for saying that Baghdad needed to change policies towards its neighbours.

"He (Muasher) is a false witness...His statement does not go beyond those we have been used to hear from the White House spokesman, state deparatment spokesman or U.S. ambassador to the United Nations," the ruling Baath party newspaper al-Thawra said in a front-page editorial.
Muasher said on Monday Iraq had to change what he called its aggressive posturing against neighbouring states if it wanted to regain the trust of the international community.
He said meeting U.N. requirements on disarmament was not enough for a comeback by Baghdad. Iraq needed, he said, to pay war reparations and meet other U.N. demands.
"The first thing to be noted about Muasher's statement is his repetition of allegations contained in statements by U.S. officials, both in letter and spirit," Thawra said.
It said the Jordanian people would be the first to turn against Baghdad if it decided to change what the newspaper described as "Iraq's principled stands".
Muasher also called on Baghdad to raise its "political language...to a level where its neighbours don't feel under any threat."
"We would like to explain to Mr Muasher that Iraq's political language is based on principled stands which concern independence, sovereignty and national and pan-Arab rights.

"We believe the Jordanian man in the street will be the first among those to be angry with us and denounce us if we gave up our principles and conformed with Muasher and his political language," Thawra said.
Jordan's Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti said on Sunday Jordan wanted Iraq to "take steps, legal and political, to reassure world public opinion" about its intentions.

Jordan, which refused to join a U.S.-led military coalition which expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait in 1991, says it is in disagreement with Iraqi President Saddam Hussein's policies towards the United Nations and neighbouring countries.
But it is also trying to play down the political differences in favour of trade benefits it expects to reap from Iraq's food- for-oil deal with U.N. which went into effect on Tuesday.

King Hussein met Iraqi Foreign Minister Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf on Friday and Kabariti met Iraqi Trade Minister Mohammed Mehdi Saleh on Monday to discuss supplying Baghdad with food and medicine under the U.N. deal.
